fixes.explanation: Yes, baker. Joseph brings in his father Jacob and presents him before Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and Jacob blesses him. Then verse 10 says Jacob blessed Pharaoh again before he departed. Two blessings in one visit. I can barely get through a visit without dropping something on the carpet.

Reuben, the firstborn! I see why you grabbed him, since his name leads the whole list (Genesis 46:8). Firstborn gets first pick of everything in my kitchen, including the dough. But this time the scout is Judah, sent ahead to Joseph to get directions to Goshen (Genesis 46:28). Reuben stays with the wagons.

Benjamin, Joseph's full brother, born to Rachel like him (Genesis 46:19). I get it, a brother going to a brother just feels right. But verse 28 says Jacob sent Judah ahead to Joseph for directions to Goshen. Benjamin rides along with the family. Think of Judah as the one who runs ahead to check the map while everybody else is still loading the wagons.

Yes, baker. Joseph prepared his chariot and went to meet his father, and then the text says he presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely. So no polite wave from a distance. He holds his father and cries hard. I think seeing a son he thought was gone, now in front of him, is a whole lot of feeling in one moment.

Good thinking, but land ownership never comes up in what Joseph says. His reason is in verse 34: “…since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.” It all comes down to how the Egyptians feel about shepherds. That's why the brothers' honest answer about their work gets them a place of their own in Goshen.

175 is a real number in Genesis. It's how long Abraham, Jacob's grandfather, lived (Genesis 25:7). But here Jacob says, “My travels have lasted 130 years…” That's his own number, and it's lower. Same family, different road.
